nodes.chainStep: Glucose, blood beta-hydroxybutyrate, venous gas, electrolytes (anion gap, potassium), urea, creatinine, osmolality, blood count; ECG
nodes.why: The initial samples are glucose, electrolytes, a venous gas, a blood count and ketones. Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is the recommended ketone test for diagnosis and monitoring: urine ketones underestimate early and overestimate late, and are not used to call resolution. A venous gas is enough. The anion gap (sodium minus chloride and bicarbonate; over 12 fits DKA) is second line, useful where ketones cannot be measured. Effective osmolality (2 x sodium + glucose, both in mmol/L) sorts out HHS. The diagnosis rests on glucose or known diabetes, ketones and acidosis, not on HbA1c.

nodes.chainStep: Search for the precipitant: examination for infection, ECG, blood cultures, urinalysis, chest x-ray if indicated, pregnancy test when relevant; medication and insulin history
nodes.why: Infection is the commonest trigger worldwide, and missed insulin the other big one; MI, stroke, pancreatitis and drugs, SGLT2 inhibitors among them, also precipitate crises. Every patient is examined for infection and ischemia and has an ECG, which also shows hyperkalemia. Antibiotics follow clinical, laboratory or radiological evidence of infection. Abdominal pain is common in DKA itself and is investigated further if it does not settle as the dehydration and acidosis resolve.

nodes.chainStep: 0.9% saline or balanced crystalloid 500 to 1,000 mL/h for the first 2 to 4 hours (JBDS: 1 L in the first hour); smaller boluses for older adults, heart failure or dialysis
nodes.why: Without renal or cardiac compromise, the consensus runs isotonic saline or a balanced crystalloid at 500 to 1,000 mL/h for the first 2 to 4 hours and corrects the deficit over 24 to 48 hours. Saline is the UK default, 1 L in the first hour; balanced crystalloids resolve DKA faster with less hyperchloremic acidosis. Older adults, heart failure and dialysis get smaller boluses, such as 250 mL, with frequent reassessment. Hypotonic saline is not a first fluid, dextrose joins the saline rather than replacing it, and slower fluid did not change neurologic outcomes in the large pediatric trial.

nodes.ask: Fluids running. Before the insulin starts?
options: Potassium level, and confirm the patient is passing urine
Start insulin now; check potassium at the 4-hour draw
Give 40 mmol of potassium to everyone before any insulin

nodes.chainStep: Serum potassium (and urine output) before insulin; ECG for hyperkalemia changes
nodes.why: Total body potassium is depleted even when the serum level is normal or high, and insulin, correction of acidosis and fluid all drive it down. The level before insulin decides whether insulin starts and how much potassium goes in the fluid, which needs adequate urine output. Bicarbonate raises the risk of hypokalemia.

nodes.note: Pediatric note: ISPAD 2022 reports clinically overt cerebral injury in 0.5 to 0.9% of pediatric DKA with 21 to 24% mortality, more often in younger children and new-onset diabetes, and linked to bicarbonate. Children follow ISPAD, not this adult pathway: fluid before insulin, insulin 0.05 to 0.1 U/kg/h at least 1 hour after fluids start, no IV insulin bolus, and mannitol or hypertonic saline at the bedside with the dose calculated when several risk factors are present.

Ketoacidosis with a normal glucose, no diabetes and heavy drinking: alcoholic ketoacidosis, not DKA. Its treatment is not in this pathway's sources.
Cerebral edema during DKA treatment: hyperosmolar therapy at once, airway support, imaging once treatment has started, ICU. Not walked further in this version.

DKA resolved: fluid first, potassium checked before insulin and replaced with it, fixed-rate insulin, dextrose once glucose is under 250, bicarbonate only under pH 7.0, then subcutaneous insulin with an overlap, the trigger treated, education and follow-up.

results.trigger: Chest x-ray: right middle lobe pneumonia. ECG sinus rhythm, no ischemia.
results.dx: Glucose 820 mg/dL (45.6 mmol/L), beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.5 mmol/L, venous pH 7.34, bicarbonate 22; sodium 142, chloride 106: anion gap 14. Effective osmolality 330 mOsm/kg. BUN 48 mg/dL (urea 17.1 mmol/L), creatinine 1.8. Total osmolality (2 x Na + glucose + urea) 347. Potassium 4.6 mmol/L; passing urine.
results.hhs_glu: 1 L saline in the first hour, then about 500 mL/h: glucose 820 to 610 mg/dL over 4 hours, then 610, 605 and 608 on three hourly checks; positive balance 2.8 L; ketones 0.4.
results.hhs_osm: 2 hours on insulin 0.05 units/kg/h: glucose 605 to 290 mg/dL (33.6 to 16.1 mmol/L), sodium 145 to 146, urea 15 to 13 mmol/L; total osmolality 339 to 321, about 9 an hour.

cases.label: DKA not resolved at 24 hours
cases.vignette: 35-year-old man with type 1 diabetes who skipped insulin for 2 days while he could not eat, after 3 days of vomiting. BP 116/72, HR 96, alert. Weight 72 kg.

results.front: Airway clear, alert; BP 116/72, HR 96, RR 26.
results.trigger: Skipped insulin for 2 days because he was not eating; no fever, chest and urine clear; ECG normal.
results.dx: Glucose 452 mg/dL (25.1 mmol/L), beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.0 mmol/L, venous pH 7.12, bicarbonate 10; sodium 133, chloride 97: anion gap 26. Effective osmolality 291 mOsm/kg. BUN 28 mg/dL (urea 10.0 mmol/L), creatinine 1.3.
results.glu: Hour 5: glucose 176 mg/dL (9.8 mmol/L), ketones 2.4 mmol/L (falling 55 mg/dL and 0.52 mmol/L an hour).
results.course: Ketones falling about 0.5 an hour to hour 9; potassium 4.4; glucose 150 to 200.
results.resolve: Hour 24: ketones 0.9 mmol/L, venous pH 7.27, bicarbonate 16; still vomiting and not eating.

calculators.title: Insulin infusion rate

bands.text: Over 15 units/h: JBDS goes higher only on diabetes team advice

sources.where: Section 4, Insulin; Section 4, Insulin in HHS
Insulin therapy, weight and dose table; 0 to 60 minutes, Action 4; Euglycaemic DKA

calculators.note: Short-acting insulin by estimated weight. HHS without ketoacidosis starts at 0.05; mixed DKA and HHS at 0.1. Euglycemic DKA starts at 0.1 with dextrose already running (JBDS). JBDS goes above 15 units/h only on diabetes team advice.

calculators.title: Anion gap

bands.text: Over 12: a high anion gap acidosis, fits DKA

sources.where: Diagnosis of DKA; Assessment of severity

calculators.note: Second line: ketones make the diagnosis and call resolution, and after large volumes of saline a hyperchloremic acidosis makes the gap misleading. JBDS adds potassium, (Na + K) minus (Cl + HCO3), and counts over 16 on that formula as a severity marker.

calculators.title: Effective osmolality

bands.text: Over 300: meets the HHS osmolality criterion

calculators.note: Glucose in mg/dL is divided by 18 (ADA 2009). HHS also needs glucose 600 or more, ketones under 3.0, pH 7.3 or more and bicarbonate 15 or more. A total osmolality, adding urea, over 320 also qualifies. ADA 2009 set the effective cutoff at 320.

calculators.title: Calculated osmolality (JBDS)

bands.text: Over 320: meets the total osmolality criterion for HHS
Over 350: also a JBDS reason to discuss an HDU bed

sources.where: Osmolality, sodium and glucose; Escalation of management; Care pathway p1

calculators.note: All in mmol/L. JBDS checks it every hour for the first 6 hours, aiming for a fall of 3 to 8 mOsm/kg an hour; until the urea is back it uses 2 x sodium + glucose. Urea is left out of the effective osmolality because it is an ineffective osmolyte.

calculators.title: Sodium as the glucose falls

outputs.label: Expected rise from the glucose fall
Sodium from the glucose shift alone

calculators.note: Consensus: 1.6 mmol/L for each 100 mg/dL fall. JBDS gives 2.4 for each 5.5 mmol/L (99 mg/dL), a larger rise. The rise is not a reason for hypotonic fluid; it matters only if the osmolality is not falling.

calculators.title: Potassium bands (consensus)

bands.text: Under 3.5: potassium first; insulin waits until over 3.5
3.5 to 5.0: insulin, with potassium in each liter to keep 4 to 5
Over 5.0: insulin, no potassium; recheck every 2 hours

calculators.note: Urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/h first. The doses differ: Figure 4 gives 10 to 20 mmol an hour under 3.5 and 10 to 20 mmol per liter at 3.5 to 5.0; the text gives 10 mmol an hour and 20 to 30 per liter. JBDS: 40 mmol/L at 3.5 to 5.5, none over 5.5, senior review under 3.5. At exactly 3.5, the consensus text still holds insulin until the level is over 3.5, while Figure 4 puts 3.5 in the middle band.
